report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 1 file that software creates by itself, not the authors: R history (1). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

text.text: This study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.
The Ethics Committee of the Medical Faculty of Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf has approved this study (study number: 2024-2722).

Only data that is routinely documented for billing purposes in the context of outpatient care, that has already been published, or that is made publicly available by the federal and state statistical offices will be used.
No individual data is available for this research project, meaning that no individuals can be identified.
Consequently, no consent can be obtained from individuals.

The global number of persons with diabetes has increased over the past decade, 1 a trend that is also reflected in Germany, where type 2 diabetes poses a growing public health challenge. 2, 3 As in many other countries, the majority of diabetes cases in Germany are classified as type 2, and the number of affected individuals has been rising steadily over recent years. 3 Previous projections suggest an increase in type 2 diabetes prevalence from 6.8 million persons in 2015 to between 10.9 and 14.2 million persons in 2040. 2 In line with these projections, the prevalence of type 2 diabetes in Germany was estimated at 9.5% in 2023. 3 Several studies indicate that the projected type 2 diabetes prevalence largely depends on temporal trends in the incidence of type 2 diabetes. 4 While extrapolating current incidence trends provides a foundation for estimating future prevalence, it is also essential to consider that these future prevalence trends are not socioeconomically neutral.

text.text: The burden of type 2 diabetes increasingly concentrates in populations with lower socioeconomic position (SEP).

Higher prevalence is consistently observed in socially deprived areas, where material disadvantage accumulates and reinforces health inequities. 5 Social deprivation refers to the relative lack of socioeconomic and material resources and the associated social and spatial burdens within an area. 6 For instance Evans et al. 7 have discovered that the prevalence of type 2 diabetes varied by deprivation, and that persons in the highest deprivation category were 1.6 (95% confidence interval 1.4-1.8) times more often affected by type 2 diabetes compared to persons in the lowest deprivation category. 7 In addition, a systematic review indicated that the SEP seems to be a risk factor for diabetes complications. 8 Although there is a strong association between SEP and the risk of type 2 diabetes and numerous studies project the future prevalence of type 2 diabetes in Germany, 2, 4, 9 none of these projections take the SEP into account.

text.text: Contrary to the evidence that future prevalence depends on temporal trends in the type 2 diabetes incidence, previous projections did not base their projections on observed trends in the incidence. 4, 9 Moreover, the data that informed previous projections rely on input data dating back to 2010. 4, 9 For these reasons we aimed to project the age-and sex-specific type 2 diabetes prevalence by SEP in Germany between 2022 and 2060 based on data available from 2022, including current temporal trends in type 2 diabetes incidence.

text.text: As in previous studies, 2, 4 we applied an illness-death model to project the future age-and sexspecific type 2 diabetes prevalence between 2022 and 2060.

text.text: The model describes the relationship between the prevalence 𝑝, the incidence 𝑖, the all-cause mortality 𝑚, and the mortality rate ratio (MRR) for individuals with vs. without type 2 diabetes.
Each of these quantities depend on the calendar year and age.

The temporal change in prevalence, 𝜕𝑝, is described by the following partial differential equation (PDE) . 10 The projection of type 2 diabetes prevalence is performed by solving the PDE through numerical integration.

text.text: To solve the PDE, different input data are required: age-specific prevalence and incidence of type 2 diabetes in the first year of the projection period, all-cause mortality, and MRR.

text.text: The scenarios differed regarding future trends in age-, sex-, and GISD-specific type 2 diabetes incidence.
In scenario 1, we assumed constant incidence between 2022 and 2060.
Scenarios 2-3 represent increasing, and scenarios 4-5 decreasing incidence trends until 2027 (5-year in-or decrease) and 2032 (10-year in-or decrease), respectively (Supplement 2).
Specifically, scenarios 2 and 3 extrapolated non-linear trends observed between 2014 and 2022, thereby capturing the observed increase in more recent years.
For scenarios 4 and 5, we used the linear decrease observed in the pre-pandemic period 2014-2019.
Details and visualizations of the scenarios are shown in Supplements 3-5.

To calculate the number of persons with type 2 diabetes, we multiplied the projected age-and sexspecific prevalence with the age-and sex-specific population projections from the German Federal Statistical Office. 12 For the population projection, we assumed moderate developments in future life expectancy at birth, birth rates, and migration.

text.text: To assess the robustness of our results to potentially different prevalence levels among immigrants and emigrants, we considered two alternative scenarios in sensitivity analyses.
In the first scenario, we assumed a threefold higher prevalence among persons immigrating to Germany and a prevalence one-third that of the resident population among persons emigrating from Germany.
In the second scenario, these assumptions were reversed, with a prevalence one-third that of the resident population among immigrants and a threefold higher prevalence among emigrants.
These assumptions are hypothetical, as empirically observed prevalence estimates for these groups are not available.
The projected numbers of immigrants and emigrants were based on the population projections of the Federal Statistical Office. 12

text.text: Figure 1 shows the age-specific prevalence of type 2 diabetes in Germany by sex and quintiles of the GISD for the five scenarios in the years 2022, 2040 and 2060.

text.text: All scenarios project an increasing agespecific prevalence, particularly among older age groups, followed by a decline at the oldest ages.
Moreover, the highest prevalence is consistently observed in these older populations.

In the scenario with a 5-year increase in incidence the prevalence peaks at ~83 years, lying between 26-37% among all GISD groups and both sexes in 2022, while in 2060 the prevalence peaks at ~91 years, lying between 47-68% among GISD groups and both sexes.

Decreasing and increasing scenarios incorporate declining or rising type 2 diabetes incidence until 2027 for the 5-year de-or increase and 2032 for the 10-year de-or increase, respectively, while the constant scenario assumes stable incidence from 2022 to 2060.

Scenarios with increasing type 2 diabetes incidence extrapolate the non-linear trends observed between 2014 and 2022, capturing the recent increase, whereas decreasing scenarios extrapolate the long-term linear decrease in incidence.
Higher socioeconomic deprivation was associated with higher age-specific type 2 diabetes prevalence with the largest difference between the highest and lowest GISD group.

In the scenario with a 5-year increase in type 2 diabetes incidence, the projected age-specific prevalence in 2060 is 68% for men and 63% for women in the highest GISD group, and 52% for men and 47% for women in the lowest GISD group, corresponding to the peak prevalence at about age 90.

It is also observed that the prevalence of men is higher than that of women in early years, but that these differences diminish in the increasing incidence scenarios, reflecting the observed steeper increase in women in recent years (Supplement 5).

text.text: In the scenario with a 5-year increase in incidence, the total number of cases among women increased from approximately 3.8 million in 2022 to 8.0 million in 2060.

A comparable increase was observed among men, with numbers rising from about 4.5 million to 7.8 million over the same period, resulting in a total increase from 8.3 million cases in 2022 to 15.8 million in 2060.

In addition to these general trends, a closer look at the prevalence and prevalence ratios (PRs) (Table 2) highlights the extent of the projected increase in the burden of type 2 diabetes between 2022 and 2060 when comparing the highest and lowest GISD groups.

text.text: The PRs reveal a growing relative disparity between the highest and lowest GISD quintile over the projection period.
In 2022, women in the highest GISD group had a 31% higher prevalence compared to those in the lowest group.
By 2060, this difference is projected to increase to 41% assuming a 5year increase in incidence.
A similar pattern was observed among men, with a ratio between the highest and lowest GISD quintiles increasing from 24% in 2022 to 39% in 2060.

Sensitivity analyses showed that, under the rather extreme scenarios considered, migration could have a substantial impact on projected type 2 diabetes prevalence and the future number of persons with the disease (Supplement 6-9).
However, the projected socioeconomic inequalities remained largely unchanged (Supplement 9).
As the actual prevalence among immigrants and emigrants is unknown, the extent and direction of any potential impact on our projections remain uncertain.

Based on an illness-death-model using the most recently available representative data, we projected future age-and sex-specific type 2 diabetes prevalence and the number of persons with type 2 diabetes, as well as socioeconomic inequalities measured by the GISD, in Germany between 2022 and 2060.
Across all considered projection scenarios, prevalence was projected to increase from 8.4 million in 2022 to between 11.2 and 19.2 million in 2060.

Inequalities in prevalence tended to increase in scenarios with increasing type 2 diabetes incidence and were rather stable in scenarios with decreasing incidence, with increasing variation between GISD quintiles over time, particularly in scenarios with rising incidence.
Our findings are in line with previous studies reporting increasing prevalence and number of persons with type 2 diabetes.

Baumert et al. 17 considered a total of 14 scenarios, with scenarios 1-5 corresponding to those described in Tönnies et al. 4 Similar to our results, they projected higher prevalence of diagnosed type 2 diabetes by 2050, driven by declining excess mortality and, in particular, increasing incidence.

Across all projection scenarios, an increase in the number of persons with type 2 diabetes was observed, with the magnitude of the increase depending on the duration of the assumed rise in incidence.
Both studies applied the same illness-death-model as used in our analysis.
However, neither of them accounted for SEP.
Despite this difference, their total numbers are comparable to ours, with previous projections estimating 10.9-14.2 million cases by 2040 and approximately 11.0 million cases by 2050.

text.text: Our findings highlight the crucial role of incidence in determining future type 2 diabetes prevalence.

Targeted prevention strategies could therefore substantially reduce future prevalence, particularly in socially deprived regions, underscoring the need for measures that address socioeconomic disparities.

Such measures could include promoting healthier lifestyles, for example by adding more green spaces in deprived areas to encourage physical activity 19 , or by adjusting taxes on different foods 20 to promote healthier dietary habits. 19 The projected increase in type 2 diabetes prevalence in Germany implies a substantial increase in future healthcare needs.

text.text: As the number of persons living with type 2 diabetes grows, so will the demand for medical care, diabetes management, and longterm monitoring. 21 This trend is expected to place a significant financial burden on the healthcare system, given the high costs associated not only with diabetes itself but also with its numerous comorbidities, such as cardiovascular diseases or neuropathy. 22, 23 Consequently, maintaining and improving the quality of care will be essential to prevent complications and ensure equitable access to effective treatment, particularly in light of persistent and increasing health inequalities.

text.text: Furthermore, demographic change will likely exacerbate these challenges: the German population is ageing, and older adults have a higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes and other chronic conditions.

At the same time, the healthcare workforce is ageing as well, with many physicians approaching retirement age, which may further strain healthcare capacity. 24 Overall, the combination of increasing Type 2 diabetes prevalence, population ageing, and limited healthcare resources underscores the urgent need for preventive measures and strategic healthcare planning to ensure sustainable diabetes care in the coming decades.

text.text: A key strength of this study lies in the use of incidence trends derived from statutory health insurance data, which cover approximately 85% of the German population. 11 The remaining 15% are either privately insured or, to a lesser extent, uninsured individuals.

text.text: Private health insurance is generally associated with better health outcomes, higher SEP, and improved access to healthcare compared to statutory insurance. 25, 26 Our findings therefore reflect the majority of the German population; however, as privately insured individuals are not included, projections for the total population may be slightly overestimated.

text.text: Furthermore, the model captures the dynamic interplay between prevalence, incidence, and mortality, all of which vary by calendar year and age.
In addition, the model can be extended to include socioeconomic differences as measured by the GISD.

This is the first study, which includes the SEP in projections of future type 2 diabetes prevalence in Germany, allowing us to explicitly quantify socioeconomic inequalities across GISD quintiles and identify the particularly high future burden in highly deprived regions.
Despite these strengths, the following limitations should be noted.
Although the incidence trend used covers almost a decade, it is still too short to reliably estimate long-term developments.
More robust assumptions about future trends would require data over a longer period.
To address this limitation, we modelled different scenarios for future incidence trends.
Determining which scenario is most likely, however, remains speculative.
The increase in type 2 diabetes incidence observed from 2019 onwards, particularly between 2020 and 2022, may be partly related to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Although healthcare utilization declined during lockdown periods, lifestyle changes such as reduced physical activity, weight gain, and altered dietary habits may have contributed to a genuine rise in new type 2 diabetes cases. 27 In addition, postponed routine check-ups and delayed diagnoses could have led to an apparent increase once healthcare access normalized.

text.text: GISD quintiles and type 2 diabetes incidence were based on the 2019 distribution and assumed constant over the observation period.
Consequently, potential socioeconomic changes are not reflected.
Nevertheless, the GISD enables analyses of health inequalities in Germany when individual-level SEP data are unavailable.
However, county-level GISD may not fully capture individual SEP.
Overall, our findings indicate a substantial increase in type 2 diabetes prevalence in Germany between 2022 and 2060.
The future burden will depend not only on the continuation of current incidence trends but also on sex and on SEP.
Socioeconomic inequalities in prevalence are expected to widen if current trends persist, with highly deprived regions bearing a disproportionate future burden.
The magnitude of this increase largely depends on how long upward trend in type 2 diabetes incidence continues.
Therefore, careful monitoring of incidence trends in the years following the pandemic is essential.
To prevent a further rise in socially patterned health inequalities, prevention and health promotion efforts should specifically target populations with low SEP.
